title: Count the stars (Genesis 15:1–6)
hookLine: a childless old man is told to count the stars, and believes

cards: Abram has land, a great name and a nation promised. What he doesn't have is a single child. Years have gone by since he left home, and still the tent is quiet.
So when God speaks to him in a vision and says fear not, I am thy reward, Abram finally says the hard thing out loud. What will you give me?
I'm going childless, and a servant in my house, Eliezer of Damascus, is going to inherit everything. It's the first time in the story Abram argues back. And God's answer is to take him outside.

teach.h: NUMBER THE STARS, IF THOU CANST.
teach.b: First, the sky. In the Douay-Rheims: "And he brought him forth abroad, and said to him: Look up to heaven and number the stars, if thou canst. And he said to him: So shall thy seed be."
Picture it with no city lights at all. God doesn't answer the complaint with an argument. God gives Abram something to look at.
Second, the response, one short verse: "Abram believed God, and it was reputed to him unto justice." Reputed means counted; unto justice means as righteousness.

The Hebrew verb for believed comes from the same root as amen: to be firm, to lean your weight on something. Nothing has changed yet: he's still old, the tent still quiet. He leans on the promise anyway.
Third, the line's long life. Paul quotes it to the Romans and the Galatians: Abraham believed, and it was counted to him. The Letter of James quotes it too, beside Abraham's deeds.

teach.h: PAUL AND JAMES BOTH QUOTE IT.
teach.b: Catholics read Paul and James together: a faith that is alive, and shows itself in love. Many Protestant churches stress faith alone.
In 1999, Catholics and Lutherans signed a joint declaration saying they share a basic understanding of this, while still differing on some points. Fourth, the stars.

The Letter to the Hebrews looks back: from one man, and him as good as dead, came children as many as the stars of heaven. Paul calls Abraham the father of all who believe, so Catholics call him our father in faith.
Jews and Muslims call him father too. A man who couldn't see one grandchild was asked to look up anyway.

how: Catholics call Abraham their father in faith, and Genesis 15:5–6 is read with Paul's letters in the liturgy; the Catechism presents Abraham as the model of the obedience of faith.

games.q: you're Abram, old and childless. God takes you outside, shows you the stars, and says: so shall thy seed be. nothing else has changed. what do you do?
o: ask for a sign you can hold.
games.why: "Abram believed God, and it was reputed to him unto justice." he leans his weight on the promise before anything changes.

practice: If it's night, find a window; if not, close your eyes and remember the clearest night sky you've seen, and start counting stars, slowly, until somewhere past ten you lose your place.
Let yourself lose it: the sky is big, the counting small. If you pray, name a promise you're still waiting on, and leave it up there.

wordCard.voice: Amen, the root behind Abram believed: to be firm, to lean your weight on a promise before anything has changed. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: he believed, he trusted. from the root of amen, to be firm.

carryVoice: Your line: so shall thy seed be. He leaned on it before he could see a thing. That's day three hundred forty-seven.
